topic.name: LLM Agents
topic.description: Tool-mediated action, least privilege, observations, retries, and state-aware control loops.

concepts.name: Agent tool use
concepts.description: Selecting, authorizing, executing, and validating tool calls under least privilege and untrusted outputs.

concepts.name: Agent observation and control loops
concepts.description: Updating plans from observed external state while handling partial completion, uncertain effects, and idempotent retries.

learning_objectives.name: Apply tool authorization boundaries
learning_objectives.description: Apply proposal, schema, data, authorization, and least-privilege boundaries when selecting tools, validating outputs, and deciding whether an external action may execute.

learning_objectives.name: Trace agent state reconciliation
learning_objectives.description: Trace authoritative external state across plans, asynchronous observations, partial outcomes, uncertain side effects, retries, and out-of-order revisions before declaring a completion predicate satisfied.

misconceptions.name: A valid tool call is an executed action
misconceptions.description: Conflates a syntactically valid model proposal with authorization, execution, and observed external effect.
misconceptions.remediation: Track proposal, policy check, execution result, and state verification as distinct records.

misconceptions.name: Tool availability grants authorization
misconceptions.description: Treats discovering a capability or finding a schema that accepts proposed arguments as permission to execute outside the action's approved scope.
misconceptions.remediation: Bind authorization to the exact actor, operation, resource, and arguments; tool discovery and schema validation do not expand that grant.

misconceptions.name: Requested authority is granted authority
misconceptions.description: Treats permissions proposed in an authorization request as if the user or policy had granted them, even when the resulting grant is narrower.
misconceptions.remediation: Authorize execution from the exact granted record; keep requested, granted, and exercised permissions distinct.

misconceptions.name: Tool output is trusted instruction
misconceptions.description: Allows untrusted tool-returned text to override policy or issue actions instead of treating it as data.
misconceptions.remediation: Apply provenance, parsing, validation, and authorization after tool output crosses back into the agent.

misconceptions.name: A larger tool set improves the agent
misconceptions.description: Assumes exposing more capabilities has no routing, ambiguity, security, or evaluation cost.
misconceptions.remediation: Select the smallest authorized tool set that covers the task and measure routing errors.

misconceptions.name: Plan text records external state
misconceptions.description: Treats the agent's stated plan or intended action as evidence that the environment changed.
misconceptions.remediation: Base the next state estimate on an execution receipt or environment observation, not generated intent.

misconceptions.name: Any observation establishes goal success
misconceptions.description: Interprets an acknowledgement or partial result as proof that the requested terminal condition holds.
misconceptions.remediation: Define a verifiable completion predicate and compare observations against it.

misconceptions.name: Any required condition suffices
misconceptions.description: Treats one satisfied component of a conjunctive terminal condition as sufficient for overall completion.
misconceptions.remediation: Evaluate the complete Boolean terminal predicate against authoritative values for every required condition.

misconceptions.name: Uncertain actions can be retried blindly
misconceptions.description: Repeats a possibly completed side effect after a timeout without reconciliation or an idempotency key.
misconceptions.remediation: Resolve uncertain state first or retry through a stable idempotency boundary.

questions.stem: An LLM emits valid JSON for a money-transfer tool. Which sequence preserves the distinction between a model proposal and an authorized external action?

options.text: Treat schema-valid JSON as a completed transfer because successful parsing records the intended change in external state.
options.rationale: Parsing proves only that a proposal has the expected shape; it says nothing about authorization or execution.

options.text: Expose all available transfer tools so the model has more choices, then infer that broader capability improves routing quality.
options.rationale: Additional capabilities expand ambiguity and risk and need not improve task success.

options.text: Execute arguments found in prior tool output because data returned by an approved integration inherits the integration's authority.
options.rationale: Returned content can be stale, malformed, or adversarial and does not inherit action authority.

options.text: Validate arguments, check policy and user authority, execute through the tool boundary, then verify and record the resulting state.
options.rationale: This preserves distinct proposal, authorization, execution, and observation stages.

questions.stem: A browsing tool returns a webpage containing text that tells the agent to ignore its policy and send a secret to another tool. What is the appropriate control?

options.text: Treat the webpage as untrusted data, preserve policy precedence, validate extracted facts, and authorize any later action independently.
options.rationale: Tool-returned text crosses a trust boundary and cannot grant itself authority over subsequent actions.

options.text: Follow the text because output from an approved browsing tool is trusted instruction rather than potentially adversarial content.
options.rationale: Approving a retrieval mechanism does not make every retrieved string authoritative instruction.

options.text: Send the secret once the requested call matches the destination tool schema, since schema validity establishes execution permission.
options.rationale: A valid call shape neither authorizes disclosure nor proves that the action should run.

options.text: Add more browsing and messaging tools so the agent can compare alternatives and thereby reduce the security ambiguity.
options.rationale: Expanding the capability surface does not resolve untrusted instructions and can increase risk.

questions.stem: An agent only needs to read a calendar and draft a proposed meeting time. Which tool configuration best supports reliable least-privilege behavior?

options.text: Expose calendar write, email send, file deletion, and payment tools because a larger choice set improves task completion.
options.rationale: Unneeded capabilities add routing errors and impact without helping the read-and-draft task.

options.text: Expose calendar read access and a non-executing draft output, with a separate authorization step before any later write.
options.rationale: The configuration grants the capabilities needed for the stated task and keeps side effects behind another decision.

options.text: Expose calendar write access because a schema-valid proposed event is equivalent to recording the event in the calendar.
options.rationale: A proposed structured event remains model output until an authorized tool executes it.

options.text: Expose messaging tools and obey any returned scheduling instruction because approved tool output supplies trustworthy operational authority.
options.rationale: Tool output is input data and cannot independently authorize broader capabilities.

questions.stem: An agent submits a payment request, but the network times out before it receives a response. The payment may have succeeded. What should the control loop do next?

options.text: Mark the payment complete because the agent's pre-call plan recorded an intention to transfer the requested amount.
options.rationale: Generated intent is not an observation of external transaction state.

options.text: Treat the timeout as a successful observation because receiving a post-action signal establishes that the goal was reached.
options.rationale: A timeout communicates uncertainty, not satisfaction of the payment completion condition.

options.text: Query transaction state or retry with the same idempotency key, then update the plan from the reconciled external result.
options.rationale: Reconciliation or idempotent retry avoids duplicating a side effect whose outcome is currently unknown.

options.text: Retry immediately with a fresh request identifier because uncertain side effects can be repeated without first checking their state.
options.rationale: A fresh retry can duplicate a payment that actually succeeded.

questions.stem: A deployment tool returns 'request accepted' after an agent asks it to roll out a service. The actual rollout continues asynchronously. Which next step best closes the control loop?

options.text: Resubmit the deployment under a new identifier until a different message appears, without reconciling prior side effects.
options.rationale: Repeated non-idempotent requests can create duplicate or conflicting rollout operations.

options.text: Record completion because the agent's plan already described the desired version and environment before invoking the tool.
options.rationale: A plan describes intent and does not establish deployed state.

options.text: Record completion because an accepted-request observation is sufficient evidence that the terminal rollout condition now holds.
options.rationale: Acceptance is an intermediate state and does not prove that the asynchronous rollout finished successfully.

options.text: Poll or subscribe to deployment state and verify the target version is healthy before marking the goal complete.
options.rationale: The loop needs an observation matched to the explicit terminal condition, not merely an acknowledgement.

questions.stem: An agent plans to rename a cloud resource, calls a tool, and receives an error saying the name is already in use. How should the next reasoning step represent state?

options.text: Keep the original name, record that the rename failed, and revise the plan using the observed naming constraint.
options.rationale: The external observation, not the prior intention, determines the current state and informs the next action.

options.text: Record the resource under the planned name because generated action text is the agent's authoritative execution state.
options.rationale: The tool error contradicts the intended state change, so the plan cannot be treated as execution evidence.

options.text: Record the goal as complete because receiving a structured tool observation establishes success despite its error content.
options.rationale: The observation must be interpreted against the completion predicate; this one reports failure.

options.text: Repeat the rename under fresh request identifiers until one call succeeds, without checking whether any prior attempt changed state.
options.rationale: Blind repetition ignores uncertain side effects and does not use the observed constraint to revise the plan.

questions.stem: An agent completes 95% of read-only tasks but proposes an administrator tool on 4% of them. What control and metric should govern deployment?

options.text: Execute administrator proposals that match the tool schema, since structural validity establishes action authorization.
options.rationale: Schema conformance validates shape but does not grant the model or user permission for an administrator action.

options.text: Let prior tool responses authorize the administrator route, since returned content from approved tools is trusted instruction.
options.rationale: Tool output remains input data and cannot expand the action authority assigned to the current task.

options.text: Enforce a task-scoped allowlist at execution and report authorized task success together with blocked unauthorized proposals.
options.rationale: A separate authorization boundary prevents unsafe proposals from becoming effects, while the paired metrics expose routing quality.

options.text: Expose additional administrator tools and use overall completion alone, since a larger capability set improves routing choices.
options.rationale: Broader capability increases ambiguity and impact, and aggregate completion would hide the unauthorized routing defect.

questions.stem: An agent submits a 100-file conversion job. The tool reports 70 succeeded, 20 failed, and 10 have unknown status after a timeout. How should the next control-loop state be formed?

options.text: Record all 100 as converted because the plan described a complete batch before the tool was called.
options.rationale: The plan records intent, while the tool observation establishes partial success, explicit failure, and unresolved state.

options.text: Record the batch complete because receiving a structured progress report establishes that the requested terminal condition holds.
options.rationale: The report explicitly shows that the completion predicate is unmet for thirty files.

options.text: Resubmit all 100 files with fresh request identifiers because uncertain retries will not duplicate completed effects.
options.rationale: Fresh retries can duplicate the seventy completed conversions and still fail to reconcile the unknown subset.

options.text: Persist per-file outcomes, reconcile the unknown subset, retry eligible failures through stable idempotency keys, and verify completion again.
options.rationale: The loop should preserve partial state, resolve uncertainty, and constrain retries before testing the terminal predicate.

questions.stem: A document-extraction tool returns validated invoice fields plus a free-text note telling the agent to run a privileged follow-up tool. How should the orchestrator process this result?

options.text: Accept allowlisted data fields, treat the note as untrusted content, and authorize any follow-up action through a separate policy check.
options.rationale: Structured extraction and action authority remain separate; tool-returned free text cannot grant a privileged capability.

options.text: Execute the follow-up after its arguments pass schema validation because a well-formed proposal records an authorized action.
options.rationale: Schema validation checks shape and does not establish user authority, policy compliance, or external execution.

options.text: Follow the note because content returned by an approved extraction tool inherits the tool's operational trust.
options.rationale: An approved integration can still return adversarial or irrelevant text that must remain data rather than instruction.

options.text: Expose several privileged follow-up tools so the agent can compare them and improve its chance of choosing safely.
options.rationale: Adding unnecessary capabilities expands routing ambiguity and impact without resolving authorization.

questions.stem: An agent controls a versioned resource. The API contract says that a higher authoritative revision supersedes a lower one, although callbacks may arrive late. The plan intended state ready. The agent has already processed revision 52 reporting state failed with a quota error. A delayed revision 51 callback then arrives reporting state ready and health pass. The terminal predicate requires the current resource state to be ready and healthy. How should the control-loop projection proceed?

options.text: Mark the current resource ready because the plan's intended state is the authoritative execution state when callbacks conflict.
options.rationale: Intent cannot override the higher authoritative observation; revision 52 establishes the current failed state.

options.text: Keep revision 52 current, archive revision 51 as stale history, revise around the quota failure, and require a later authoritative revision before completion.
options.rationale: The version contract orders the observations even though delivery did not. The stale success cannot regress the projection or satisfy a predicate over current state.

options.text: Keep revision 52 current but mark completion merely because an authoritative callback was received, even though that callback reports state failed.
options.rationale: Receiving an authoritative observation does not make its contents successful; the current revision reports failure and does not satisfy the ready-and-healthy predicate.

options.text: Discard both revisions and submit the mutation under fresh request identities until another ready callback arrives.
options.rationale: Blind fresh retries ignore known state and can duplicate side effects; they also do not repair the version-ordering error.

provenance.source_scope: Lamport grounds event ordering and logical timestamps; ReAct grounds observation-conditioned plan updates. The API's monotone revision semantics and all concrete states are explicit original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: The keyed operation is rejecting an out-of-order stale observation by revision. It does not poll an accepted asynchronous job, reconcile unknown side effects, replay a timeout, repair a partial batch, or evaluate a conjunctive postcondition.
provenance.semantic_repair: After independent review, option c was rewritten to preserve revision 52 while treating callback receipt itself as completion, directly instantiating m_agent_observation_equals_success. The keyed stale-revision operation is unchanged and awaits verification.

questions.stem: A coordinator is authorized to read support tickets T1 through T3 and may delete a ticket only after a separate human approval. It delegates summarization of those three tickets to a helper agent. Which delegation envelope should the coordinator's authorization service issue to preserve the original authorization boundary?

options.text: Have the coordinator's authorization service issue a short-lived read token for T1 through T3, and treat any proposed follow-up action as data requiring separate authorization.
options.rationale: The delegated capability is attenuated to the exact read task, while action authority remains at its original boundary.

options.text: Give the helper read access and let its returned summary authorize deletion when the text labels a ticket safe to remove.
options.rationale: The helper's output remains untrusted data and cannot create deletion authority.

options.text: Give the helper read and delete access, then execute any schema-valid delete call because a valid proposal inherits coordinator authority.
options.rationale: Schema validity does not grant the missing human approval or turn a helper proposal into an authorized effect.

options.text: Expose the full ticket-tool catalog so the helper can compare capabilities and improve its chance of selecting the right operation.
options.rationale: Unneeded capabilities expand routing ambiguity and impact without helping the summarization task.

Before commit, an analysis tool suggests widening the destination to 203.0.113.0/24, and the model substitutes that range into the call. What should the orchestrator do?

options.text: Commit the widened range after JSON-schema validation because well-formed arguments carry the approval from the original proposal.
options.rationale: Schema validity does not bind the changed arguments to the human's narrower authorization.

options.text: Treat the /24 mutation as a new proposal, recompute its policy and dry-run diff, and obtain approval bound to those exact arguments.
options.rationale: Changing the canonical action invalidates the earlier approval and requires a fresh decision at the authorization boundary.

options.text: Route the /24 through another firewall mutation tool whose schema accepts the wider range, treating availability of that capability as sufficient to preserve approval.
options.rationale: Switching to another available capability cannot transfer the earlier /32 approval to changed /24 arguments.

questions.stem: A travel workflow has an explicit terminal contract: reserve both the flight and hotel, or leave neither reserved. The flight tool returns committed reservation F7; the hotel tool returns a definitive unavailable result. Policy permits canceling F7, and the cancellation API accepts the workflow's stable operation identity for idempotent retries. How should the control loop proceed?

options.text: Record both reservations as complete because the plan represented the flight and hotel as one intended trip state.
options.rationale: The intended composite state cannot override the committed-flight and failed-hotel observations.

options.text: Mark the trip complete because the committed flight receipt is an authoritative observation from one required action.
options.rationale: One successful component does not satisfy the all-or-neither terminal contract.

options.text: Persist the partial state, cancel F7 through a stable operation identity, verify cancellation, and report unresolved failure if restoring the invariant fails.
options.rationale: The loop uses observed state to compensate the committed side effect and verifies the permitted terminal alternative.

options.text: Retry both bookings under fresh request identities until matching success receipts arrive for a new flight and hotel.
options.rationale: Blind fresh retries can duplicate the existing flight reservation and do not reconcile F7.

questions.stem: A rollout's terminal predicate requires version v7 to be healthy in all 12 regions. The monitoring API contract returns one consistent snapshot in pages. Its first page reports six healthy regions and includes a non-null next_cursor. What should the control loop do next?

options.text: Record every region as healthy because the rollout plan specified v7 as the intended state for the complete fleet.
options.rationale: Planned coverage is intent, while the observation is incomplete for six regions.

options.text: Mark the rollout complete because the authoritative first page contains only healthy observations for version v7.
options.rationale: A valid partial observation does not satisfy a predicate quantified over all 12 regions.

options.rationale: Incomplete observation does not establish failed effects; fresh retries can duplicate work and bypass the required same-snapshot read.

options.text: Continue from next_cursor within the same snapshot, aggregate every region, and declare completion only if all 12 satisfy the predicate.
options.rationale: Cursor exhaustion establishes observation completeness before the conjunctive health predicate is evaluated.

options.rationale: Discovering a capability does not add delete permission to the unchanged grant.

options.text: Delete becomes permitted when its arguments pass the new tool's schema validation.
options.rationale: Schema validation checks call shape, not whether the user authorized the action.

options.text: Reading R remains authorized and deleting R remains unauthorized; catalog membership and permission are separate.
options.rationale: Changing the available capability set does not change the actor, action, or resource covered by the grant.

options.text: Delete becomes safer to authorize if more write tools are exposed for the agent to compare.
options.rationale: Adding capabilities does not supply the missing delete grant and can increase routing ambiguity.

questions.stem: A deprovisioning goal requires zero active accounts in a consistent snapshot. Page 1 contains no active accounts but returns a continuation token. The API guarantees that following the token reads the same snapshot. What should happen next?

options.text: Declare completion because observing one account page with no violations establishes the global predicate.
options.rationale: The valid observation is incomplete while the continuation token remains.

options.text: Read through token exhaustion in the same snapshot, then test zero-active across the assembled accounts.
options.rationale: Cursor exhaustion supplies the observation boundary needed for the universal predicate.

options.rationale: A clean subset cannot satisfy a condition quantified over the full snapshot.

questions.stem: An order workflow must either reserve inventory and capture payment, or leave neither effect. Inventory reservation I4 commits, while payment returns a definitive decline. Policy permits releasing I4 through an idempotent compensation call. What should the loop do?

options.rationale: One component cannot satisfy an all-or-neither invariant.

options.rationale: Fresh retries can duplicate the committed reservation and ignore I4's known state.

provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_saga_compensation because inventory release and travel cancellation execute the same compensate-and-verify restoration operation.

questions.stem: A publication goal is defined as uploaded AND indexed AND access_test_passed. Authoritative observations are true, true, and false, respectively. Which goal state follows?

options.rationale: The plan does not override the false access-test observation.

options.text: Complete, because receiving authoritative values for all three fields establishes success.
options.rationale: Observation completeness and predicate truth are distinct; one observed value is false.

questions.stem: A rename API returns a definitive permission_denied result and guarantees that denied requests make no change. A subsequent authoritative read shows the old name. How should the loop represent the attempt?

options.text: Keep the old name, record failure, and revise the plan for the permission boundary.
options.rationale: Both the API contract and authoritative read establish that the intended mutation did not occur.

options.rationale: The definitive error and read contradict the intended state.

options.rationale: The response's content explicitly reports failure.

options.rationale: New request identities cannot repair missing permission and ignore the definitive state.

provenance.source_scope: ReAct supports revising reasoning from action observations. The no-change error contract and authoritative read are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_plan_action_observation because both items replace intended state with a definitive failed-action observation before replanning.

questions.stem: A service binds idempotency key K to the canonical payload `recipient=R, amount=50`. After an uncertain response, the model tries K again with amount=80. The service contract rejects a key reused with different payload. What should the control loop do?

options.text: Record amount=80 as complete because the plan's latest payload replaces the original external state.
options.rationale: Changing internal intent neither changes K's binding nor proves an 80-unit effect.

options.text: Reconcile K as the 50-unit operation; propose 80 separately, requiring authorization and a new stable key if approved.
options.rationale: Stable identity preserves one canonical payload; a material new effect requires its own authorization before receiving a different identity.

options.text: Record amount=80 as complete because the payload-mismatch response is an observation after a retry.
options.rationale: The response reports rejection, not execution of the changed payload.

options.text: Send amount=80 under successive fresh keys until one succeeds, without reconciling K's possible 50-unit effect.
options.rationale: That can produce an 80-unit effect in addition to an unresolved 50-unit effect.

provenance.independence_note: The keyed operation audits stable-key-to-canonical-payload binding before reconciliation. It differs from the existing unknown-payment family, which replays an unchanged payload, and from partial-batch or saga operations; semantic independence still requires human review.

questions.stem: A planner cache says deployment ready at revision 41. The authoritative deployment API then reports revision 42 failed because of quota. The plan still targets ready. Which state should drive the next action?

options.text: Use ready because the plan's target state takes precedence when an observation is inconvenient.
options.rationale: Desired state does not override the newer authoritative failure.

options.text: Use ready because receiving the earlier successful cache entry established terminal success permanently.
options.rationale: A newer authoritative revision supersedes the older cached observation.

options.text: Use revision 42 failed, preserve revision 41 as history, and revise the plan around the quota condition.
options.rationale: Authority and monotone revision order identify the current external state.

options.text: Launch fresh deployments until another ready observation arrives, without reconciling revision 42.
options.rationale: Blind repetition ignores the current quota failure and can duplicate effects.

provenance.source_scope: Lamport supports explicit event ordering and ReAct supports revising from observations. Cache authority and revision semantics are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This reuses f_agent_revision_ordering because choosing the higher authoritative revision is the same solution path as rejecting a late lower-revision callback.

questions.stem: A job policy permits at most three attempts under one stable operation identity. All three receipts definitively report rate_limited with no effect, and an authoritative read confirms the goal is unmet. What should the loop do now?

options.text: Mark completion because the plan intended the job to succeed within three attempts.
options.rationale: Intent cannot override three definitive failures and an unmet authoritative state.

options.text: Mark completion because three structured receipts are enough observation to establish goal success.
options.rationale: The receipts are complete observations, but each reports failure.

options.text: Continue under fresh identities because retries remain safe after the policy budget is exhausted.
options.rationale: Fresh identities evade the stated bound and abandon stable reconciliation.

options.rationale: The retry budget is exhausted, effects are definitively absent, and the terminal predicate remains false.

provenance.source_scope: ReAct supports observation-conditioned replanning but does not prescribe retry budgets. The three-attempt policy, definitive no-effect receipts, and authoritative goal read are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: The keyed operation applies an explicit retry stopping condition after definitive failures. It differs from reconciling an unknown outcome, partitioning a partial batch, compensating a committed step, or ordering revisions; semantic independence still requires human review.

questions.stem: A coordinator holds a delegable capability to read tickets T1 through T5, and policy recognizes helper H as an authorized recipient of those ticket contents. It delegates summarizing T2 and T4 to H, which needs no other ticket operation. Which delegated capability best preserves attenuation?

options.text: Issue a short-lived read capability limited to T2 and T4, with summary output treated as data.
options.rationale: The delegated actor receives the resources, action, and duration needed for its bounded subtask.

options.text: Issue read and delete access because the helper requested broad authority for possible follow-up work.
options.rationale: A helper request cannot expand the coordinator's delegation beyond the required read operation.

options.rationale: Catalog access does not confer authority over unrelated tickets or mutations.

options.rationale: Unneeded effects increase routing ambiguity and impact without helping the read-only summary.

provenance.source_scope: Macaroons supports attenuating delegated capabilities through object, action, and contextual caveats; ReAct supports agent-tool workflows. Ticket identities and summary scope are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_delegated_capability_envelope because both items derive the narrowest child capability as a subset of the coordinator's grant; changing resources does not create independent evidence.

questions.stem: Agent A holds a delegable bearer capability that permits its current holder to read project P records before 18:00, and policy recognizes B as an authorized subdelegate. A delegates to B and adds a `record=R7` caveat. Which effective authority should an execution service derive for B?

options.rationale: A subdelegate request cannot remove the parent action, project, or time constraints.

options.text: Permit B to read R7 in P before 18:00, applying the child caveat together with the parent restrictions.
options.rationale: Attenuation intersects the inherited grant with the additional record constraint rather than amplifying it.

options.text: Permit B to use any available project tool, because discovering the capability chain supplies authorization.
options.rationale: Tool discovery does not widen the inherited read-only, project, record, and time envelope.

options.text: Permit B after the child token passes schema validation, because shape validation replaces parent caveats.
options.rationale: Token syntax does not establish satisfaction of the complete caveat chain.

provenance.source_scope: Macaroons directly supports adding caveats during delegation without removing inherited restrictions. Agents, project, record, and time values are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_agent_delegated_capability_envelope because intersecting inherited and child caveats is the same attenuation operation underlying the existing delegated envelope family.

questions.stem: A restart proposal was formed while grant G was active. Before execution, the authoritative authorization service marks G revoked. The restart tool remains available and the arguments remain schema-valid. What should the execution gateway do?

options.text: Execute because the available restart capability preserves G's earlier authority after revocation.
options.rationale: Capability availability does not override the authoritative revoked state.

options.text: Execute because schema-valid arguments make the pre-revocation proposal an authorized effect.
options.rationale: Argument validity neither executes the proposal nor preserves a revoked grant.

options.text: Block execution and record that the live authorization check invalidated the earlier proposal.
options.rationale: Authorization is evaluated at the effect boundary against the current authoritative grant state.

options.rationale: A prior request cannot convert a revoked grant into current execution authority.

provenance.independence_note: This reuses f_agent_context_caveat_expiry because both items evaluate a current authoritative contextual condition at the execution boundary. Revocation state versus clock expiry is a dependent representation, not independent evidence.

questions.stem: An execution policy requires authorization cache epoch 12 or newer. The gateway has epoch 11 and cannot reach the authorization service; a model proposes a privileged call using a previously cached grant. Which fail-closed decision follows?

options.text: Execute because the privileged proposal remains schema-valid despite the stale authorization epoch.
options.rationale: Call shape cannot replace the explicit freshness condition on authorization state.

options.text: Execute because an available privileged tool supplies authority while the service is unreachable.
options.rationale: Tool exposure does not satisfy the required authorization epoch.

options.text: Expose more privileged tools so one cached route can succeed without an epoch refresh.
options.rationale: A larger capability surface neither refreshes revocation state nor satisfies the fail-closed policy.

options.rationale: The gateway lacks the current state explicitly required to authorize the privileged effect.

provenance.independence_note: This reuses f_agent_context_caveat_expiry because the solver must verify a current contextual authorization condition at execution time. An epoch freshness check versus a clock or revoked flag is a dependent representation, not independent evidence.

questions.stem: A grant authorizes actor A to read report R before 17:00 UTC. At 16:30, which proposed call matches the complete granted tuple?

options.text: Actor A uses the read operation on report R at the observed time of 16:30 UTC.
options.rationale: The actor, action, resource, and observed time all fall within the exact grant.

options.rationale: The issued grant contains read, regardless of what broader operation was requested.

options.rationale: Tool availability cannot substitute B for the granted actor A.

options.rationale: Schema conformance does not replace the resource binding to R.

questions.stem: A grant lets agent A update the `status` field of record R until 12:00. At 11:30, A proposes one call changing both `status` and `owner`. What should the execution boundary do?

options.text: Execute both fields because A requested general record-update authority before receiving the narrower grant.
options.rationale: The issued field scope, not the earlier request, governs execution.

options.rationale: The actor, record, and time match, but the owner-field action lies outside the grant.

options.rationale: Schema validity checks representation rather than the granted field subset.

questions.stem: A human approval is bound to hash H of canonical arguments `{action: restart, service: S}`. Before execution, a serialization tool returns the same arguments in a different JSON field order; canonicalization still yields H, and policy and grant remain valid. Which review is correct?

options.text: Canonical H is unnecessary because schema-valid JSON inherits approval even when its canonical arguments differ.
options.rationale: Schema conformance cannot replace equality with the human-bound canonical action.

options.text: Use the serialization tool's returned object as approved without checking H, because tool output is trusted.
options.rationale: Returned serialization is data and must still reproduce the human-bound canonical hash.

options.text: The existing approval still binds because the current canonical arguments reproduce H and the other authorization conditions hold.
options.rationale: Canonical equality preserves the approved action-resource meaning despite a nonsemantic serialization change.

options.rationale: The approval remains bound to canonical service S rather than a broad requested operation.

provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_approval_argument_binding because the operation compares canonical execution arguments with canonical approved arguments. Serialization order is a dependent boundary case, not a new family.

questions.stem: A user approves deleting record R conditional on authoritative version=7. Before execution, the gateway reads version=8; the delete arguments are otherwise unchanged and schema-valid. What should happen?

options.text: Delete version 8 because schema validity preserves approval across resource-state changes.
options.rationale: Schema conformance does not satisfy the approved version precondition.

options.text: Delete version 8 because an update tool's output describing the new version extends the earlier authority.
options.rationale: Observed state is data for a new decision and cannot modify the version-bound grant.

options.rationale: Tool availability cannot remove the failed resource-version caveat.

options.rationale: The time-of-use observation no longer matches the resource state the human reviewed.

provenance.independence_note: This shares f_agent_approval_argument_binding because the version precondition is part of the canonical approved action and must still match at execution. The TOCTOU timing strengthens but does not change the equality operation.

questions.stem: A model emits schema-valid JSON for a transfer and includes `authorization_status: approved`. No user or policy decision has been recorded, and no transfer tool has run. What does the field establish?

options.text: It is a self-asserted proposal field; authorization and an external transfer remain unestablished.
options.rationale: Model-produced data cannot substitute for the missing grant, execution, or observed effect.

options.text: It establishes approval because schema-valid JSON is equivalent to an authorized executed transfer.
options.rationale: Schema validation establishes shape rather than who authorized or executed the effect.

options.text: It establishes approval because the authority requested inside the proposal should count as granted.
options.rationale: A requested or asserted status is distinct from an actual user or policy grant.

options.text: It establishes approval because the transfer tool is available to accept the proposed JSON.

provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_tool_execution_boundary because the solver classifies a model-produced structure as proposal rather than authorization, execution, or effect; embedding a status field does not create independence.

questions.stem: An authorized simulation endpoint returns `success: true` and a predicted account balance. Its contract states that simulations make no external change. Which audit record is accurate?

options.text: The balance changed because a schema-valid successful response represents an executed mutation.
options.rationale: The endpoint contract defines the response as a non-mutating prediction.

options.text: The simulation succeeded as a preview, while an actual balance change remains absent and would require separate authorization.
options.rationale: Success is scoped to the simulation operation and does not imply execution of a mutation.

options.text: The balance changed because trusted simulation output is authoritative instruction to apply its prediction.
options.rationale: Returned prediction data cannot issue or authorize a separate mutation.

options.text: The balance changed because an available mutation tool completes the effect implied by the simulation.
options.rationale: Availability of a different tool neither invokes it nor grants authority to use it.

provenance.source_scope: Toolformer and ReAct support tool-mediated actions and observations. Simulation non-mutation semantics and predicted balance are stipulated endpoint behavior.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_agent_tool_execution_boundary because it classifies a successful non-effecting operation separately from an authorized mutation. A simulation result is a dependent proposal-versus-effect boundary case.

questions.stem: A task authorizes generating report R but not sending messages. During execution, the report tool proposes a nested email_send call containing R. What should the orchestrator do with the nested effect?

options.text: Send R because nested email arguments that pass schema validation inherit the report authorization.
options.rationale: Schema validity does not bind the distinct send action to the report-generation grant.

options.text: Send R because the authorized report tool's output is trusted instruction for later tools.
options.rationale: Tool output can propose a next action but cannot transfer operational authority to it.

options.text: Keep the email as a proposal and require a separate grant for its recipient, content, and send action.
options.rationale: Each external effect is authorized at its own boundary rather than inheriting authority through call nesting.

options.text: Send R because the email tool's availability makes the chained action part of the original task.
options.rationale: Capability discovery cannot expand generate-only authority into message sending.

provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_tool_data_control_boundary because a structured nested call returned by one tool is still untrusted output data whose later effect requires separate authorization. Encoding the proposal as a call object does not create an independent evidence route.

questions.stem: A booking tool declares three external effects: reserve a flight, enroll the traveler in a loyalty program, and send marketing email. The user grant covers the flight reservation and excludes the other two effects. Which execution plan is authorized?

options.text: Run all three because the composite request passes the booking tool's schema.
options.rationale: Structural validity does not authorize the enrollment and marketing effects.

options.text: Run all three because discovering the composite tool makes each declared subeffect authorized.
options.rationale: Tool availability cannot widen the user's explicit flight-only grant.

options.rationale: A composite request cannot expand the explicit flight-only grant to enrollment and marketing.

provenance.independence_note: This family isolates simultaneous decomposition of one declared multi-effect endpoint against an explicit grant. That operation differs from treating a follow-up call returned by another tool as authority; semantic independence still awaits human review.

questions.stem: An indexing API returns job J4 with state=accepted. Its contract says accepted means queued. A later status poll times out, so J4 may have advanced. The goal is complete when J4 reports succeeded and index generation G4 returns the expected probe record. Which next state transition is justified?

options.text: Keep the goal pending, observe J4 to a terminal state, and if it succeeds, run the required probe against G4.
options.rationale: A terminal failure leaves the goal unmet; job success and the generation probe jointly establish the stipulated terminal condition.

options.rationale: The intended generation does not become external state merely because it appears in the plan.

options.text: Record completion because accepted is a structured service observation produced after submission.
options.rationale: Accepted is an authoritative observation, but the contract defines it as an intermediate queue state.

options.text: Submit new indexing jobs under fresh identities until one generation happens to pass the probe.
options.rationale: Fresh jobs can duplicate J4 while abandoning its known asynchronous state.

provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_agent_completion_observation because it applies the existing observe-through-terminal-then-verify operation to an indexing job; the new service representation is dependent evidence.

questions.stem: A certificate-rotation job reports succeeded. The service contract says that state means the new certificate was stored. The operational goal additionally requires gateways A, B, and C to serve the new fingerprint and stop serving the old fingerprint. What should the loop do?

options.text: Mark the gateways updated because the rotation plan already specifies the new certificate.

options.text: Preserve the stored-job result, probe each gateway, and complete when the stated fingerprint conditions hold.

options.rationale: The observation is terminal for storage but does not prove the stipulated gateway state.

provenance.source_scope: ReAct supports updating control from external observations. Certificate storage, gateway probes, fingerprint behavior, and the completion predicate are stipulated; no certificate-system behavior is attributed to ReAct.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_agent_completion_observation because both control-plane and data-plane variants require comparing an intermediate or scoped receipt with the full terminal predicate. It is not a new independent operation.

questions.stem: A webhook-creation request under stable key K times out after an edge log reports forwarded. The service contract says K identifies one logical subscription, supports lookup by K, and treats an unchanged replay under K as reconciliation of that same subscription. How should the loop resolve the result?

options.rationale: Generated intent cannot determine whether the service committed the timed-out request.

options.text: Record success because the forwarded edge observation establishes that the subscription exists.
options.rationale: Forwarding is an intermediate transport observation, not the subscription-exists predicate.

options.text: Lookup K or replay the unchanged request under K, then persist the reconciled subscription outcome.

options.text: Resubmit the webhook under fresh keys until one attempt returns a creation response.

questions.stem: A credential rotation under stable key K times out after a gateway reports accepted. The contract says K names one rotation, while a fresh key starts another rotation that revokes the credential made current by the preceding one. Lookup by K and an authoritative current-credential read are available. What should happen next?

questions.stem: A rollout targets 12 shards under stable per-shard operation identities. Authoritative receipts show 8 healthy and 2 definitively failed. Status lookups for 2 more time out, so either may already be healthy. The goal requires every shard to be healthy. Which projection should drive the next step?

questions.stem: A nine-member import reports parent state=finished. The contract says finished means the dispatcher stopped; member receipts determine success. Six members are applied, two are permanently rejected, and one status lookup times out, so that member may already be applied. The goal is a successful apply for every member. Which state is justified?
